messages.subject: Overplotting, with each point neatly lined up (not jittered)
parts:
I want to plot some data. Not very much data but many points fall on
top of one another. Jitter scrambles things too much. The data is very
granular so stripchart would do the job better and I would include the
parameters method="stack", offset=.8. But I want to use ggplot2
because I plan to bring in another layer.

Just came across this group and delighted it exists.

parts:
Hi Farrel, 

I can't quite make the plot you are aiming for, but perhaps my 'just about' answers will set you on the right track ;)
--
# Make up some data ans set up the plot
df <- data.frame("value"= rpois(20, 3), "grp"=rep(c("one", "two"), each=10))
p.dot  <- ggplot(df, aes(grp, value))

#controlled jitter
p.dot + geom_point(position=position_jitter(height=0, width=0.2))

# or dodge
p.dot + geom_point(position=position_dodge(width=0.2))

You might also consider giving up plotting each data point separately:

p.bar <- ggplot(df, aes(value))
p.bar + geom_bar() + facet_grid(grp ~ . )

Hope that goes some way to helping you out.

Cheers,
David

messages.subject: RE: Overplotting, with each point neatly lined up (not jittered)
parts:
just a workaround, it requires some tuning ...


library(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame(x = gl(3, 10, labels = c("A", "B", "C")), y = rpois(30,
lambda = 1))
scp <- function(df)
{
df$xn <- as.numeric(df$x)
df$ind <- with(df, y / (2 * max(y)) + xn)
df <- df[order(df$ind), ]
df$xr <- df$xn
df$ind <- (c(1, diff(df$y)) == 0 & c(1, diff(df$xn)) == 0)
c <- 1
while ( any(df$ind) )
{
df$xr[df$ind] <- df$xr[df$ind] + 1/30
df$xr[!df$ind] <- df$xr[!df$ind]
df$ind <- (c(1, diff(df$y)) == 0 & c(1, diff(df$xr)) == 0 &
c(1, diff(df$xn)) == 0)
}
qplot(x = xr, y = y, data = df) +
scale_y_continuous(name = "Variable") +
scale_x_continuous(name = "Factor",
limits = c(0.5, length(unique(df$xn)) + 0.5),
breaks = unique(df$xn), labels = levels(df$x))
}
scp(df)

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Overplotting, with each point neatly lined up (not jittered)
parts:
Hi:

Here are a couple of ideas for strip charts in ggplot2. A strip chart is,
in essence, a 'scatterplot' of a categorical variable with a numeric one.

# Fake data:
df <- data.frame(gp = rep(LETTERS[1:5], each = 20), y = rnorm(100))

# Basic strip chart:
p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = y, y = gp))                # scaffolding
p + geom_point()                                       # add points as a layer

# One alternative to overplotting: alpha transparency
p + geom_point(alpha = 0.5)

# Another alternative: jittering
p + geom_point() +
     geom_jitter(position = position_jitter(height = 0.1))  # more points, more jitter...

# Third alternative: reduce the size of the points (default size in geom_point = 2)
p + geom_point(size = 1.4)

# Note: trying to combine point size reduction with jittering does not work well...
p + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
     geom_jitter(position = position_jitter(height = 0.1))

# Can do a few other things, like removing the gray background and some of the
# gridding:
p + geom_point(size = 1.4) + theme_bw() +
   opts(panel.background = theme_blank())

# To get rid of the vertical axis and produce a little bit thicker horizontal grid,
# try
p + geom_point(size = 1.6) + theme_bw() +
    opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank()) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1:5, size = 1.1, alpha = 0.1)

Hopefully this will give you enough to get started...

HTH,
Dennis

parts:
How about this:

# your data

df <- data.frame(gp = rep(LETTERS[1:5], each =8), y =
sample(1:4,40,replace=TRUE))

# calculate offsets
df <- ddply(df, .(y, gp), transform, offset = (1:length(gp)-1)/20)
qplot(gp, y, data=df) + stat_identity(aes(as.numeric(gp)+offset)) + theme_bw()

Probably you need to adjust the number "20" to fit your plot size and
point size.

Xie Chao

messages.subject: Re: Overplotting, with each point neatly lined up (not jittered)
parts:
Hi Xie:

Thanks for the insight.

This is what I sent to the OP earlier. Forgot to copy to the list...
df <- data.frame(gp = rep(LETTERS[1:5], each =8), y = sample(1:4,40,replace=TRUE))
p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = y, y = gp))

jit <- position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0)
p + geom_point() + geom_jitter(position = jit) + theme_bw() +
   opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank())

This jitters around the intersection point, but is not completely satisfying aesthetically.

With your idea of offsetting the points, I wrote a small function to center
the offsets around zero and then to do another ggplot, as follows:

oset <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  v <- if(n > 1) seq((-n + 1), n - 1, by = 2) else 0
  v/20
 }
df2 <- ddply(df, .(y, gp), transform, offset = oset(gp))
p2 <- ggplot(df2, aes(x = gp, y = y))
p2 + geom_point() + theme_bw() + stat_identity(aes(as.numeric(gp) + offset)) +
     xlab("gp") + opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank())

Hopefully this will satisfy our OP.

HTH,
Dennis

It worked perfectly even though I do not have a jot of a clue what
actually went on.
Do you have the patience to teach me what happened?
The offset transformation simply gives each row a unique number. The
offset works best when the divisor is number of rows. It then later
gets added back to the numeric version of the categorical variable
which is sitting in the data as a factor.
What on earth does the aes do? It puts dots neatly next to one another
even if that particilar point would not have the perfect spacing if
one just took as.numeric(gp)+offset. My rows were in no particular
order. Somehow, qplot was using stat_identity to go get a uniqe value
for each point and then regardless of the the value was lining them up
next to one another. How did it do that? The documentation says that
stat_identity creates a layer but what layer?

messages.subject: Re: Overplotting, with each point neatly lined up (not jittered)
parts:
Sorry for making the stuff sounds complicated. There is no magic in
stat_identity, you can safely replace it with geom_point. So there are
two layers in your plot --- the original over-plotted geom_point and
the adjusted geom_point. You can not see the over-plotted points
because they are covered by the adjusted points...

OR
If you prefer a cleaner plot rather than shorter code:

# your data
df <- data.frame(gp = rep(LETTERS[1:5], each =8), y =
sample(1:4,40,replace=TRUE))
# calculate offsets
df <- ddply(df, .(y, gp), transform, offset = (1:length(gp)-1)/20)

# plot gp+offset vs y,
qplot(as.numeric(gp)+offset, y, data=df) +
scale_x_continuous(
breaks=1:nlevels(df$gp),
# re-label the x-axis so that it looks like a discrete variable
labels=levels(df$gp),
minor_breaks=NA) + theme_bw()

Again, you need to adjust the number "20".

Xie Chao

>> >> Hi:
>>
>> >> Here are a couple of ideas for strip charts in ggplot2. A strip chart is,
>> >> in essence, a 'scatterplot' of a categorical variable with a numeric one.
>>
>> >> # Fake data:
>> >> df <- data.frame(gp = rep(LETTERS[1:5], each = 20), y = rnorm(100))
>>
>> >> # Basic strip chart:
>> >> p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = y, y = gp))                # scaffolding
>> >> p + geom_point()                                       # add points as a
>> >> layer
>>
>> >> # One alternative to overplotting: alpha transparency
>> >> p + geom_point(alpha = 0.5)
>>
>> >> # Another alternative: jittering
>> >> p + geom_point() +
>> >>      geom_jitter(position = position_jitter(height = 0.1))  # more points,
>> >> more jitter...
>>
>> >> # Third alternative: reduce the size of the points (default size in
>> >> geom_point = 2)
>> >> p + geom_point(size = 1.4)
>>
>> >> # Note: trying to combine point size reduction with jittering does not
>> >> work well...
>> >> p + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
>> >>      geom_jitter(position = position_jitter(height = 0.1))
>>
>> >> # Can do a few other things, like removing the gray background and some of
>> >> the
>> >> # gridding:
>> >> p + geom_point(size = 1.4) + theme_bw() +
>> >>    opts(panel.background = theme_blank())
>>
>> >> # To get rid of the vertical axis and produce a little bit thicker
>> >> horizontal grid,
>> >> # try
>> >> p + geom_point(size = 1.6) + theme_bw() +
>> >>     opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank()) +
>> >>     geom_hline(yintercept = 1:5, size = 1.1, alpha = 0.1)
>>
>> >> Hopefully this will give you enough to get started...
>>
>> >> HTH,
>> >> Dennis
